precepts.text: The Philistine lords understood this even without the book; it is a lesson for us to apply today.
precepts.point: This is the wisdom we have to apply today. There is always an outsider who dresses like us, talks like us, and gets himself accepted among our people; yet even the Philistines knew: he might be good to you, he might be serving you, but do not trust your enemy.
precepts.why:
“Never trust thine enemy: for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness.” The Philistine lords understood this even without the book.

Achish told David, “thou hast been upright”, and “I have not found evil in thee since the day of thy coming unto me unto this day: nevertheless the lords favour thee not.” Though David was good in his sight “as an angel of God”, “the princes of the Philistines have said, He shall not go up with us to the battle.”

One of the things to take from this reading is that they have more sense than we do. The lords of the Philistines said, No, he cannot go to battle with us, because we will always be looking over our shoulders wondering if he is going to change his mind and go back unto his people.

This is the wisdom we have to apply today. There is always an outsider who dresses like us, talks like us, and gets himself accepted among our people. Yet even the Philistines knew: he might be good to you, he might be serving you, but do not trust your enemy.

precepts.why: The term angels is a reference to men on earth as well; when you read it, read it in context. “And Achish answered and said to David, I know that thou art good in my sight, as an angel of God:” As an angel of God.

note.label: Bishop Nathanyel | Revelation 2 Message to the 7 Churches

precepts.why: “thou art good in my sight, as an angel of God”. Achish is speaking to David, a man. Angel can mean a human messenger. That is how the angel addressed in Ephesus is the man leading that church, not one of the heavenly angels.

points: The Philistines gathered all their armies to Aphek, and Israel pitched by a fountain in Jezreel. David and his men passed on in the rearward with Achish, and the princes of the Philistines demanded, What do these Hebrews here?

Achish vouched for David: he has been with me these days, or these years, and I have found no fault in him since he fell unto me. But the princes were wroth and said, Make this fellow return to his place; let him not go down with us to the battle, lest in the battle he be an adversary to us. For wherewith should he reconcile himself unto his master? should it not be with the heads of these men?
The princes remembered the song: is not this David of whom they sang one to another in dances, saying, Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands?

Achish told David, As the Lord liveth, thou hast been upright, and thy going out and thy coming in with me in the host is good in my sight; I have not found evil in thee. Nevertheless the lords favour thee not: return, and go in peace. David protested, What have I done, that I may not go fight against the enemies of my lord the king? But Achish answered that though David was good in his sight as an angel of God, the princes had said he shall not go up with us to the battle. So David and his men rose up early and returned into the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

One of the things to take from this reading is that they have more sense than we do. The lords of the Philistines told Achish, No, he cannot go to battle with us, because we will always be looking over our shoulders wondering if he is going to change his mind and go back unto his people.

This is the wisdom we have to apply today. There is always an outsider who dresses like us, talks like us, and gets himself accepted among our people; yet even the Philistines knew: he might be good to you, he might be serving you, but do not trust your enemy.
